executive_summary: The Canadian dollar enters September 2026 caught between the strongest Canadian macro print in three years and the most severe bilateral trade rupture since the North American free-trade era began. USD/CAD trades at 1.39045, the CAD-inverted convention meaning a rising pair is a weaker CAD; the loonie is 0.31% weaker against the US dollar over twelve months but outperformed eight of its ten G10+SGD peers over the past month, gaining 1.30% on CHF, 1.12% on JPY and 0.76% on USD [11][37]. Canada posted 3.3% annualised Q2 GDP growth — the fastest since early 2023 and a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada's own 2.5% call — alongside a C$8.8bn current account surplus, the first since 2022 and the largest since 2005, and a 6.4% unemployment rate that is a two-year low [7][8][9][26]. Against that, the United States imposed 50% Section 338 tariffs on approximately US$20bn of Canadian goods on 2026-08-22 with no expiry date and no negotiating calendar, Canada retaliates on 2026-09-08, and Washington has signalled a further escalation to 50% on autos, trucks, parts and steel from 2027-01-01 [23][24][25][11]. The valuation case is unambiguous — Canada's BIS real effective exchange rate of 95.71 is the second cheapest in the G10+SGD complex behind only the yen, and the combined CFTC speculative short of 131,035 contracts remains far beyond the -80,000 threshold the currency has historically treated as extreme [13]. The carry case is unambiguous in the other direction: the CA-US two-year spread sits at -119bp and the ten-year at -102bp, and the futures-implied cost of holding CAD against USD is -166.3bp annualised, while Fed funds futures price a 58% probability of a Federal Reserve hike on 2026-09-16 against a 3% probability that the Bank of Canada moves on 2026-09-02 [11][18][22]. Our tactical weighted score is +0.007 and our strategic score is -0.114: we are deliberately Neutral over two to four weeks, where the short-covering squeeze, cheap valuation and record external surplus exactly offset the carry penalty and the Fed asymmetry, and mildly Bearish CAD over one to six months, where the market's ~65% probability of a 2026 Bank of Canada hike — against the Bank's own survey median of Q3 2027 — is the mispricing we intend to fade [19][22][27].

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since late July has been a data-driven CAD recovery colliding with a policy-driven CAD threat. From 2026-07-28 to 2026-08-21 the dominant narrative was hawkish repricing: Canadian ten-year yields rose to 3.76%, the highest since April 2024, retail sales and factory sales beat, and the market pushed late-2026 Bank of Canada hike odds toward 65% on the back of 3.0% headline CPI. That regime broke on 2026-08-22 when trade talks collapsed and 50% Section 338 duties took effect; ten-year yields fell to 3.62% within three sessions before recovering to 3.746% by 2026-08-31. Volatility has stayed remarkably contained through both phases, with twenty-day realised at 4.6% and three-month implied at 4.748%, which tells us the market is treating the tariff shock as a bounded sectoral event rather than a macro regime break; the dominant cross-asset driver remains the CA-US rate differential, which the Bank of Canada itself named as the cause of the currency's depreciation.

tactical.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 68 to 65 after adversarial verification found the Canadian ten-year quoted at 3.74% rather than 3.746% on the cited page, and an unreconciled one-day basis difference between the cached US constant-maturity curve (2026-08-27) and the live US ten-year (2026-08-31). The Bank of Canada's overnight rate target is 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.50% and the deposit rate at 2.20%, unchanged since the October 2025 cut and held for a sixth consecutive meeting on 2026-07-15 [1][5]. That places CAD joint sixth of the ten rate-setting currencies in the benchmarking set, level with EUR at 2.25%, and 137.5bp below the Federal Reserve's 3.625% midpoint. The tactical problem is not the level but the direction of the gap over the next four weeks: bond markets price a 3% probability that the Bank hikes on 2026-09-02 and all 35 Reuters-polled economists forecast a hold, while Fed funds futures price a 58% probability of a 25bp Federal Reserve hike on 2026-09-16, up from 36% before Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole address [18][22]. The expected-value arithmetic is therefore asymmetric by construction: the CA-US policy gap has a 58% chance of widening to 162.5bp and only a 3% chance of narrowing to 112.5bp inside the tactical window. The front-end market already reflects part of this — the CA-US two-year spread is -119bp (Canada 3.01% live 2026-08-31 versus US 4.20% cached 2026-08-27) and the ten-year spread is -102.0bp on a like-for-like live basis [11] — but it does not reflect a Fed hike as a certainty. The Canadian curve is positively sloped at +73.0bp on 2s10s, steeper than the US +39bp, which signals that the Canadian long end has repriced with global duration rather than the front end pricing a domestic tightening cycle. Canada's own ten-year touched 3.76% on 2026-08-21, the highest since April 2024, then fell to 3.62% on the tariff escalation before recovering to 3.74% — the front end did not follow, which is precisely the pattern of a market that wants term premium, not policy tightening [11]. The Bank of Canada named this mechanism itself: "U.S. bond yields have risen, while those in Canada are little changed. This differential has contributed to the depreciation of the Canadian dollar." [5] Against this, the market's residual ~65% probability of a Bank of Canada hike by end-2026 is a genuine CAD support that has not yet unwound, and National Bank explicitly argues it is overpriced [19]. We take the bearish side because the dated asymmetry inside four weeks runs one way.

strategic.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 52 to 48 after adversarial verification corrected the Bank of Canada Market Participants Survey median from a first hike in Q3 2027 to 2.50% in March 2027, narrowing the wedge versus market pricing from roughly four quarters to one to two. Over one to six months the question is whether Canada can close a 137.5bp policy gap and a 119bp front-end gap, and the honest answer is that no credible path does so. Even the most hawkish Canadian forecasts — National Bank and Scotiabank, two of the six largest domestic banks, both calling 2.50% in October and 2.75% by December — would only narrow the policy differential to 87.5bp if the Federal Reserve stood still, and to 112.5bp if the Fed delivers the September hike that is 58% priced [18][22]. BMO, CIBC, RBC and TD all forecast 2.25% through December 2026, and TD Securities sees rates on hold before any move higher [21][22]. Rabobank argues the policy rate is already at terminal and that neither hikes nor cuts are warranted through 2027, on the grounds that trade-war demand weakness argues against hikes while core inflation near 2% argues against cuts [20]. There is no realistic six-month path in which CAD earns positive carry against USD. The Bank's own Q2 2026 Market Participants Survey has the median policy rate at 2.25% through January 2027 and reaching 2.50% only in March 2027, with 2.75% not arriving until Q3 2027 — placing the median first hike one to two quarters beyond where the OIS market currently sits [27]. An earlier draft of this dossier described that gap as four quarters; the corrected figure is one to two quarters and the strategic confidence on this factor has been reduced accordingly. That gap resolves toward the Bank far more often than toward the market, and when it does the Canadian front end reprices lower — mechanically removing CAD's best remaining rate support. Working the other way, 47% of the Reuters panel expects at least one increase by the end of Q2 2027, headline CPI at 3.0% sits at the top of the Bank's 1-3% band, and Macklem has committed publicly that "we will not let higher oil prices become persistent inflation" [4][22]. If Brent holds above US$90 and gasoline pass-through broadens into core, the hawkish path becomes live and the differential compresses fast. Confidence is set at 52 rather than higher precisely because the distribution is genuinely bimodal — the six largest Canadian banks are split four to two on direction, which is unusual and honest to reflect.

tactical.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 62 to 56 after adversarial verification found three second-order errors in the Q2 national accounts detail — the Q1 revision was 0.0% to +0.1% quarter on quarter rather than a revision from a contraction, the +2.3% referred to engineering structures after two declining quarters rather than aggregate business investment after five, and corporate incomes rose 9.6% rather than 9.7%. The Canadian data flow into September is the strongest of any G10 economy relative to its own recent history, and it is the single largest CAD-positive force in this dossier. Real GDP grew 3.3% annualised in Q2 2026, the fastest quarterly pace since early 2023 and a full 80bp above the Bank of Canada's own 2.5% projection, while Q1 was revised up from 0.0% to +0.1% quarter on quarter [7], retiring the recession narrative — note that secondary coverage characterised this as a revision "from a contraction", which the Statistics Canada release does not support, and the Statistics Canada figure is used here [7][26]. The composition was broad: exports +3.6% with passenger car and light truck shipments up 27.0%, investment in engineering structures +2.3% after two consecutive quarters of decline, and residential investment +2.5% as resale activity returned to positive growth following two contracting quarters, with regional differences [7][26]. The labour market has turned: July employment rose 75,000, the unemployment rate fell to 6.4%, the lowest since July 2024 and a third consecutive monthly decline, with Ontario alone adding 52,000 [9]. Headline CPI accelerated to 3.0% year-on-year in July from 2.8% in June, reaching the top of the Bank's 1-3% control band and giving the hawkish camp its statistical footing [6]. Recent surprises have skewed positive: core retail sales beat at +0.5% against a 0.2% forecast, headline retail sales at +0.6% against 0.4%, the industrial product price index at +0.6% against -0.4%, monthly GDP at +0.3% against +0.2%, and corporate incomes at +9.6% quarter-on-quarter against a prior 1.1% (the pipeline calendar carried +9.7%; the Statistics Canada figure of +9.6% is used and the 0.1pp discrepancy is flagged). Leading indicators corroborate: the Ivey PMI printed 55.1 in July with a 56.2 consensus for 2026-09-04, and the manufacturing PMI's prior reading was 53.5 — both comfortably expansionary. The offsets are real and cap our confidence: the Bank's preferred core measures are CPI-trim at 1.9% and CPI-median at 2.0%, averaging exactly to target, CPI excluding gasoline has been pinned at 2.2% for three consecutive months, and wage growth decelerated to 2.8% year-on-year from 3.3% [6][9]. The entire headline acceleration is gasoline, up 25.7% year-on-year on the Strait of Hormuz blockade [6].

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has priced the Q2 GDP beat and the 6.4% unemployment rate into a ~65% probability of a Bank of Canada hike by year-end, so the good news is not free. Our edge is on the two dated releases inside the window: the 2026-09-04 labour force survey carries a consensus of only +15.8k after July's +75.1k, and the 2026-09-14 CPI faces a gasoline base effect that will be much less favourable than July's. We think the labour print beats a lowered bar and headline CPI holds at or above 2.9%, which extends the hawkish repricing for two to three more weeks before the tariff drag becomes visible.

strategic.analysis: The Q2 data describe a quarter that ended in June, and everything published since points the other way. Statistics Canada's advance estimate for July showed output essentially unchanged at 0.0% — and that was measured before the 2026-08-22 Section 338 tariffs and before Canada's own 2026-09-08 counter-measures take effect [7][22]. The Bank of Canada's own July projection has Canadian GDP growing just 0.7% for 2026 as a whole, which after a 3.3% annualised Q2 implies materially sub-trend outcomes in the second half, and 1.8% in each of 2027 and 2028 [2][5]. The inflation picture decays mechanically from here: with CPI-trim at 1.9% and CPI-median at 2.0%, the entire 100bp gap between headline 3.0% and core 2.0% is gasoline, and the EIA projects Brent averaging US$85/bbl in Q3 2026 and US$87/bbl for the year with most regional production returning toward pre-conflict levels in early 2027 [32]. As that base effect rolls off through Q4 and Q1, headline converges down toward core, not core up toward headline — which is exactly the Bank's own stated projection of a return to 2% by early 2027 [5]. Wage growth at 2.8% and falling from 3.3% removes the second-round mechanism entirely; unit labour costs are not generating services inflation. The Bank's July deliberations were explicit that "continued excess supply and slow growth in unit labour costs were putting downward pressure on other prices, particularly for services excluding shelter", and that housing-related services and rent inflation had slowed on lower demand amid slower population growth [3]. On growth, the tariff arithmetic bites: US$20bn of goods at 50% duties is 5.2% of the US$382bn Canada shipped to the United States in 2025, the Bank estimates approximately 2 million Canadian jobs rely on goods exports to the US, and Canadian manufacturing already shed more than 32,000 jobs between January 2025 and January 2026 [23]. Canada's retaliation is self-inflicted cost on top: Carney called it "reluctant" precisely because it raises Canadian prices and reduces choice [23]. Note that CBC reported the affected US tariff coverage as "hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion" in Canadian dollars against the US$20bn figure used here; the two are reconcilable at prevailing exchange rates but the currency basis differs between sources and is flagged [24].

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance flips from Bullish to Bearish between horizons because the two horizons are looking at different quarters. The tactical window is dominated by the Q2 GDP beat, the 6.4% unemployment rate and the two September releases that follow from that momentum; the strategic window is dominated by the July 0.0% flash, the Bank's own 0.7% full-year call and the arithmetic of tariffs landing on 5.2% of bilateral exports. The mechanical inflection is the arrival of post-tariff activity data — the first clean read is the October monthly GDP release covering August, and the decisive read is the Q3 national accounts in late November.

tactical.analysis: Global risk conditions are as supportive as they have been all year, and CAD is a mild beneficiary. The VIX closed at 14.51 on 2026-08-27, down 3.70 points over the preceding month, having touched 14.2 on 2026-08-17 — the lowest level of 2026 and more than 50% below the 31.65 recorded on 2026-03-27 [38]. Credit is corroborating rather than diverging: the ICE BofA US investment-grade option-adjusted spread is 79bp and the high-yield OAS is 263bp as of 2026-08-27, the latter having tightened 21bp over the month from 284bp. The S&P 500 stands at 7,670.19, roughly 16% higher year to date, and the Bank of Canada's July deliberations recorded that "global equity markets rose as investors focused less on the Middle East conflict and more on continued strong earnings in AI-related sectors" [3][11][38]. CAD's risk beta is mildly positive but structurally lower than AUD's or NZD's, because the US economic linkage anchors it — the currency brief's normal correlation of USD/CAD to the S&P 500 is -0.2 to -0.3, roughly half the sensitivity of the Antipodeans. The complication in the current regime is that the two channels through which risk normally reaches CAD are pulling apart. Oil is rising on a supply shock rather than a demand signal: Brent moved back above US$90 on 2026-08-31 after US strikes on Iran drew retaliation, and the US diesel crack exceeded US$100/bbl for the first time, an intraday record just above US$102 [33]. Supply-driven oil strength helps Canadian export revenue but hurts the global growth impulse that normally accompanies risk-on. Domestically, the TSX Composite fell 1.02% to 36,182 on 2026-08-31 even as the broad risk complex held, reflecting tariff-specific Canadian equity pressure that the global indices do not carry [11]. We stay bullish because the level of risk appetite is unambiguously supportive, while acknowledging the correlation structure has partially decoupled.

Our edge is narrow here because we agree with the level while disagreeing with the durability. We hold the bullish stance at only 55 confidence because the entry point for risk-beta length is poor, and note that the mid-August to mid-October window is historically the weakest stretch of the calendar for risk assets.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor delivers no directional signal for CAD, and we assign Neutral as a considered conclusion rather than a default. The arguments are close to exactly balanced. On the constructive side, credit spreads at 79bp investment grade and 263bp high yield are not merely tight but tightening, the AI capital-expenditure cycle that the Bank of Canada identified as "supporting economic activity in a growing number of countries" shows no sign of stalling, and the Federal Reserve's balance sheet has resumed expanding, which historically supports risk multiples [3][5][14]. On the cautionary side, a VIX at 14.51 sitting at the 2026 low is a poor base from which to underwrite six months of stability, particularly with an unresolved Strait of Hormuz squeeze and a US-Canada trade rupture that Ottawa expects to persist beyond the November midterms [23]. More importantly for this specific currency, the risk channel and the oil channel have decoupled. CAD's historical risk beta was earned in regimes where oil rose with global demand; the current oil strength is a supply constraint that simultaneously raises Canadian export revenue and suppresses the global growth that Canadian exports serve. Netting those two effects produces close to zero. The tail scenarios cut both ways and roughly cancel: a Hormuz reopening would take Brent below US$75, crushing Canadian terms of trade while boosting global risk appetite; a full closure would spike Brent above US$110, boosting Canadian revenue while triggering a global risk-off in which CAD weakens against USD anyway. Neither tail is CAD-directional. The stalemate breaks only if oil and equities re-correlate in the same direction, which would require a demand-driven move rather than the supply-driven one now in play.

As of the 2026-08-25 reference date, leveraged funds are net short 72,092 contracts (27,384 long against 99,476 short, plus 3,777 spreading) and asset managers are net short 58,943 (55,489 long against 114,432 short), for a combined speculative short of 131,035 contracts against total open interest of 329,544 [13]. Leveraged funds represent -21.9% of open interest, down from -25.3% two weeks earlier. Dealers and intermediaries sit on the other side at net long 124,930, meaning the street is warehousing the crowd's short. The weekly change is the tactical signal: against the 2026-08-18 reference date, leveraged funds covered 16,805 contracts and asset managers covered 30,552, while total open interest fell 30,041 contracts, or 8.4% — that combination of falling open interest and shrinking shorts is position liquidation, not fresh long accumulation. Compared against the cached tranche series, which had leveraged funds at -85,957 on 2026-07-07, -102,495 on 07-28 and -92,005 on 08-11 with asset managers at -108,343, -101,160 and -104,545 on the same dates, the combined speculative short has fallen from -196,550 on 2026-08-11 to -131,035 on 2026-08-25 — a 65,515-contract, 33% reduction in a fortnight. Portfolio flows reinforce the picture from a different direction: foreign investors bought a record C$80.8bn of Canadian government bonds in Q2 2026 [22].

tactical.what_is_priced: Positioning is not "priced" so much as it is fuel, and 131,035 contracts of remaining speculative short is a lot of fuel. Our edge is in reading the composition: the covering came from both leveraged funds and asset managers simultaneously while dealers reduced length, which is the profile of a genuine squeeze rather than dealer-driven rebalancing. strategic.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 58 to 55 after adversarial verification found an arithmetic error in the original statement of the speculative short as a share of open interest; the corrected figures are 39.8% on the net measure and 64.9% on gross speculative shorts. The strategic positioning read is bullish for a different reason than the tactical one: not the flow, but the stock. Even after covering 65,515 contracts, the combined speculative book is still short 131,035 contracts of Canadian dollars, equal to 39.8% of the total open interest of 329,544 — and gross speculative shorts of 213,908 contracts amount to 64.9% of open interest [13]. That is a structural overhang, and structural overhangs resolve upward over multi-month windows far more often than they deepen. The counterparty structure matters: dealers hold net long 124,930 contracts, which means the sell-side balance sheet is the natural buyer of CAD only because it has been forced to absorb the crowd's short; dealers do not add to that position at the margin, so incremental speculative selling faces a thinning bid and incremental covering faces a willing offer. Real-money flow corroborates. The record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of Canadian government bonds in Q2 2026 is not a speculative position but an allocation decision, and it arrived in the same quarter the current account swung to a C$8.8bn surplus — the first since 2022 and the largest since 2005 [8][22]. Canadian pension funds (CPPIB, OTPP and peers) are large global investors whose hedging programmes create mechanical CAD demand when foreign asset values rise, which they have with the S&P 500 up 16% year to date. Working against the bullish read: open interest of 329,544 is itself down 8.4% in a week and roughly 9.5% from the 364,104 cached on 2026-08-11, so the market is disengaging from CAD rather than re-engaging, and a shrinking open-interest base reduces the squeeze mechanics that make positioning tradeable. Nor is positioning at a genuine extreme any longer on the leveraged-fund leg, which is now inside the -80,000 threshold.

factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is stretched but less stretched than it was. For CAD, "stretched" begins around -80,000 contracts on the leveraged-fund net, per the currency brief; the combined speculative measure is far past that at -131,035, but the leveraged-fund leg alone at -72,092 has now dropped inside the threshold for the first time since early July. The trigger for a further unwind is already active — the 33% reduction over the fortnight to 2026-08-25 is the unwind, not a forecast of one. What would accelerate it is a soft Federal Reserve outcome on 2026-09-16 (42% probability) or a hawkish tone from Governor Macklem on 2026-09-02; either would force the remaining short into a market where dealers are already long 124,930 and unwilling to add. A squeeze from this base would be violent in a specific and bounded way: the last comparable episode saw leveraged-fund shorts reduce roughly 100,000 contracts, and USD/CAD ranges of 55 pips per day mean a two-week squeeze of that magnitude is a 250-350 pip move, taking USD/CAD toward the 1.3574-1.36925 fourteen-touch support shelf. The contrarian case against being bullish here is that the crowd may be right: a currency facing 50% tariffs with no expiry, negative carry of 166bp and a central bank pinned at 2.25% deserves to be shorted, and one third of the position has already covered without USD/CAD breaking 1.3800. Net signal: bullish CAD, moderately.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: On a one-to-six-month view the contrarian question is whether 131,035 contracts of speculative short represents exhaustion or conviction. The evidence favours exhaustion on the flow and conviction on the stock. Asset managers have cut their short roughly in half from -108,343 on 2026-07-07 to -58,943 on 2026-08-25, which is real-money capitulation on the bearish CAD trade; leveraged funds have cut less, from -85,957 to -72,092 over the same period, and are the more persistent short. What would trigger a full unwind is a resolution of the trade conflict — the November midterms are the only dated circuit-breaker, and Ottawa's own assessment is that no substantive deal arrives before them [23]. What would deepen the short is confirmation of the 2027-01-01 escalation to 50% duties on autos, trucks, parts and steel, which would extend the tariff regime from 5.2% of bilateral exports to a materially larger share [11]. The historical analogue is instructive: the speculative CAD short reached comparable extremes in early 2025 during the first tariff cycle and took roughly five months to normalise, with USD/CAD trading a 700-pip range in the process rather than trending. Net signal: bullish CAD, weakly — the position is a cushion, not a catalyst.

tactical.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 60 to 57 after adversarial verification could not source the 76% (2024) and 72% (2025) US export-share comparators from the cited primary release; only the approximate 70% June 2026 figure is derivable there. Canada's external accounts have just delivered the single best print in two decades, and the tactical window contains a trade balance release that can extend it. Statistics Canada reported on 2026-08-27 that the current account swung from a deficit of C$8.3bn in Q1 2026 to a surplus of C$8.8bn in Q2 — the first surplus since 2022 and the largest since 2005 — driven by a goods trade swing on record energy and auto exports [8][22]. The consensus forecast had been C$3.5bn, so this was a C$5.3bn upside surprise, the largest single beat in the August data ledger. The merchandise trade account underpins it: June's goods surplus rose from C$3.7bn in May to C$3.9bn, with total exports reaching a record C$77.5bn, a fifth consecutive monthly increase amounting to +22.8% over that run [10][40]. The composition matters for the tactical read: exports to the United States rose 0.3% and the bilateral US surplus narrowed from C$11.1bn to C$10.0bn, while the US share of total Canadian exports was approximately 70% in June 2026 (69.5% derivable from the June release), against materially higher shares in 2024 and 2025 — Canada is diversifying, slowly but measurably [10][40]. The specific 76% (2024) and 72% (2025) comparators come from secondary aggregation rather than the cited primary release and are flagged as best available. Terms of trade are supported by the energy complex: WTI at US$85.446 and Brent at US$90.135 on 2026-08-31, both up more than 2.3% on the session after US strikes on Iran, with Henry Hub natural gas at 2.9365 [11][33]. Cached levels of WTI 83.90 and Brent 88.24 on 2026-08-25 sit US$12.07 below the 100.31 Brent print of 2026-07-24, so the month has been a decline from the spike followed by a re-acceleration. The decisive tactical fact is the tariff carve-out: energy, potash, fish and critical minerals were excluded from the Section 338 duties [23]. Canada's largest export category by value is untouched by the trade war.

strategic.analysis: Verification note: confidence reduced from 62 to 58 for the same unverified export-share comparators, and because the WCS-WTI differential rests on forecast vintages rather than a live spot quote. On a one-to-six-month view the external account is the strongest structural argument for CAD in this dossier, and it survives the tariff shock better than the headlines suggest. The current account surplus of C$8.8bn in Q2 2026 is the first since 2022 and the largest since 2005; at roughly 1.1% of quarterly GDP it reverses a decade of persistent small deficits and, critically, it was achieved on goods trade rather than one-off income items [8][22]. Canada's cached Q1 current account of -0.87% of GDP already compared favourably with the United States at -2.85%, the United Kingdom at -2.84%, Australia at -3.68% and New Zealand at -3.95%; the Q2 swing puts Canada ahead of every deficit country in the benchmarking set. Terms of trade are structurally supported: the EIA projects Brent averaging US$87/bbl for 2026 with approximately 0.6 million barrels per day of Strait of Hormuz disruption persisting through the end of 2027, which is a multi-quarter, supply-side revenue transfer to non-Gulf producers [32]. Canada is a direct beneficiary and the tariff regime does not touch it — the carve-out for energy, potash, fish and critical minerals means Canada's commodity complex trades on global prices, not bilateral politics [23]. The Bank of Canada's July deliberations added that aluminium exports benefited from elevated global prices and supply shortages in Europe, and that copper and aluminium prices rose on supply constraints [3]. Financing is abundant: a record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of Canadian government bonds in Q2 funds the capital account without requiring a weaker currency to clear [22]. Against all this stand three real drags. The tariffs cover 554 product lines and US$20bn of goods, or 5.2% of the US$382bn shipped to the United States in 2025, and escalate to 50% on autos, trucks, parts and steel from 2027-01-01 [11][23]. The WCS-WTI heavy differential is projected at roughly US$12/bbl for 2026 and US$13/bbl from 2027, capping the Canadian realisation of any Brent rally — this figure derives from forecast vintages rather than a live spot quote and is flagged as best available [research §E2]. And 70% of exports still go to one increasingly hostile customer.

A 50% duty rate is arresting; 5.2% of bilateral exports with the entire energy complex exempt is not a balance-of-payments event, and Canada just posted its largest current account surplus in twenty-one years while the tariffs were being negotiated. tactical.analysis: The Bank of Canada's communication going into 2026-09-02 is deliberately two-sided, and a two-sided central bank produces no tactical signal. The July 15 statement concluded that "Governing Council judges the current policy rate remains appropriate to sustain the economic recovery and bring inflation back to the two per cent target" while adding that "uncertainty is still high" and that the Bank "is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed" — language that commits to nothing in either direction [1][5]. The Summary of Governing Council Deliberations published 2026-07-29 is more revealing and equally balanced: members "agreed to look through the direct effects of higher global oil prices on inflation" because "there was limited evidence that higher oil prices were spilling over to the prices of other goods and services", but also "agreed to reiterate in their communications that they would not let higher oil prices lead to persistent inflation" [3]. Governor Macklem said it directly in the opening statement: "We will not let higher oil prices become persistent inflation." [4] That is a hawkish commitment device attached to a dovish assessment. The deliberations also record that "there was a range of views among Governing Council members about the sustainability of the rebound beyond the near term" — an explicit disclosure of internal disagreement that reduces the informational value of any single meeting's tone [3]. This factor carries the single largest identifiable wedge in the dossier, and it resolves against CAD. Market pricing carries a ~65% implied probability of a Bank of Canada hike by end-2026 [19]. The Bank's own Q2 2026 Market Participants Survey, published in late July, has the median policy rate at 2.25% through January 2027 and reaching 2.50% only in March 2027, with 2.75% not arriving until Q3 2027 — a gap of roughly one to two quarters between what the OIS curve pays for and what the Bank's surveyed counterparties actually expect [27]. Confidence on this factor has been reduced from 58 to 50 as a result. Central bank credibility determines which side converges, and the Bank of Canada is among the most credible and transparent institutions in the G10: quarterly MPR forecasts, a published Summary of Deliberations, explicit neutral-rate estimates in the 2.75-3.25% range, and a track record of following through. When a credible central bank and the market disagree on the timing of a first move, the market converges more often than the Bank does. The mechanism by which it happens is already visible in the Bank's own reasoning. The July deliberations state that inflation "was expected to ease to about 2½% in the second half of 2026 before reaching the 2% target in early 2027" and that "continued excess supply and slow growth in unit labour costs were putting downward pressure on other prices" [3]. tactical.analysis: The tactical window contains the highest concentration of dated binary risk of any currency in the benchmarking set, and the balance is CAD-negative. On 2026-09-08, Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect on approximately US$20bn of US imports at rates of 15-50%, covering steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and motorcycles — and the product-level list had not been published as of the valuation date, which means the market cannot have priced its composition [11][23][25]. That is an unpriced binary inside the window. It follows the 2026-08-22 imposition of 50% US duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 on approximately US$20bn of Canadian goods across 554 tariff lines, the first presidential use of that authority since 1949, applied regardless of USMCA preferential treatment and carrying no expiry date [23][24]. Talks collapsed within hours of a Friday-afternoon expectation of a breakthrough, over the written text rather than the three named grievances; USTR Jamieson Greer confirmed no new talks are planned [23][24]. Carney's framing was explicit: asked whether Canada was at war, he said "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked." [23] The second live theatre is the Persian Gulf. The United States carried out targeted strikes against Iran in the days before the valuation date, drawing retaliatory strikes, and Brent moved back above US$90/bbl in early Asian trading on 2026-08-31 [33]. For CAD this is ambiguous rather than simply negative — higher crude raises Canadian export revenue and Canadian headline CPI simultaneously — but the volatility it injects into a currency already carrying tariff risk is not. The event-vol premium is the striking observation: 43.6-day implied vol is 4.514% against 99.6-day at 4.748%, a contango term structure with no near-term kink despite four dated events inside five weeks. Gamma into these events is cheap.

strategic.analysis: The strategic event risk is not a series of dates but a structural condition, and it is the most CAD-negative fact in this dossier. Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 permits proclamation-only tariffs without any prior investigation or hearing, and carries no time limit — unlike the IEEPA tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2026, the duties remain until a future presidential proclamation removes them [23]. There is no statutory clock forcing the parties back to the table. Ottawa's internal assessment, reported through people familiar with the government's deliberations, is that no substantive talks resume before the November 2026 midterms, and Prime Minister Carney told premiers that the support measures being designed for affected industries would remain in place "for as long as it takes, in other words, beyond the life of this U.S. administration" [23]. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew put the planning horizon at two years. The escalation path is already announced: US tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel rise to 50% from 2027-01-01 [11]. The USMCA architecture that would normally constrain this has been dismantled — the mandatory six-year review was triggered on 2026-07-01 when the administration declined to renew the agreement in its current form, US-Mexico bilateral talks are proceeding on a separate track, and Canada is conspicuously absent from that track [23]. The magnitude is bounded but the duration is not: US$20bn is 5.2% of the US$382bn Canada shipped south in 2025, and Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliation imposes a proportionally heavier burden on an economy roughly one tenth the size [23]. The Bank of Canada estimates approximately 2 million Canadian jobs depend on goods exports to the United States. The only plausible circuit-breaker inside the strategic window is the 2026-11-03 midterms, and the mechanism by which they would help — US domestic political pressure from tariff-driven cost-of-living pain, with American consumers having absorbed more than US$231bn in tariff costs between February 2025 and January 2026, roughly US$1,745 per family — is indirect and slow [23].

No rating action, review or outlook change is scheduled or pending inside the window, and there is no auction calendar stress: the record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of Canadian government bonds in Q2 2026 is the opposite of a failed-auction environment, and the Bank of Canada's own market notices in August concerned a repo general-collateral basket and a settlement fail-fee trial rather than any funding difficulty [22]. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months Canada's fiscal position becomes a modest relative-value advantage rather than a neutral. The federal debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to rise above 43% by 2027-28 before stabilising, and Canada retains the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7 — a comparison that matters because the currencies against which CAD is measured include the United States, the United Kingdom and France, all of which are carrying materially worse trajectories [35]. The market is voting with capital: C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of Canadian government bonds in Q2 2026 was a record, and that inflow arrived in the same quarter the current account swung to surplus, meaning Canada is funding itself comfortably without requiring currency depreciation to clear the capital account [8][22]. The long end is orderly: the 30-year yield at 4.15% and the 20-year at 4.02% compare with a US 30-year at 5.19% and a UK ten-year at 5.14%, so the term-premium penalty being applied to Anglo-sphere fiscal deterioration is being applied to Canada least of all [11]. Rating agencies cite effective and predictable policymaking, stable political institutions, economic resilience and monetary and fiscal flexibility, and the 2025-26 deficit was revised downward to C$66.9bn rather than upward [35]. Set against this are two real risks. The tariff support package Carney has promised is explicitly open-ended and unbudgeted, and Ottawa is designing it on the assumption it may need to cover the balance of the US administration's term — that is an uncapped commitment against a shrinking tariff-exposed tax base [23]. Provincial fiscal dynamics diverge sharply, with Alberta and Saskatchewan benefiting from elevated resource revenue while Ontario and Quebec carry the larger deficits and the larger tariff exposure. Combined federal-plus-provincial debt is materially above the federal figure alone. Confidence is held at 55 because the relative advantage is real but the absolute trajectory is deteriorating.

factors.expression_assessment: The volatility landscape is unusually informative and points in one direction: express the view through options rather than spot. Three observations drive this. First, implied volatility is cheap in absolute and relative terms. At-the-money implied is 4.514% at one month, 4.748% at three months and 4.884% at six months, and our estimated IV percentile sits in the 20th-25th percentile of the trailing year (flagged as an estimate, since no quoted implied-vol history was obtained). Second, realised volatility is outrunning near-dated implied. Twenty-day realised at 4.6% exceeds the 43.6-day implied of 4.514% by roughly 8.6 vol-basis-points. A negative variance risk premium at the front of the curve means the market is being paid less than the market is actually moving — options are cheap on a delivered basis, and directional spot trades are being rewarded. At six months the relationship reverses (4.884% implied against 4.01% sixty-day realised), so the cheapness is concentrated in near-dated maturities. Third, the term structure is in contango with no event kink. Rising implied vol from one month to six months, with four dated catalysts inside the first five weeks, is the signature of a market pricing no event premium at all. Backwardation ahead of a central bank meeting is the norm; contango into one is an anomaly and it means near-dated gamma is being sold cheaply. The skew adds the final piece. A 25-delta risk reversal of +0.113% at three months and -0.030% at six months is functionally flat. There is no CAD-put premium, which means acquiring CAD downside exposure costs almost exactly what acquiring CAD upside exposure costs. Given a Neutral tactical stance with identified event risk and a mildly Bearish strategic stance, the landscape favours owning near-dated volatility into the 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-16 events, and acquiring longer-dated CAD downside exposure while the skew charges nothing for it. Where spot expression is used, it should be sized against the negative carry: -166.3bp annualised on the futures roll is 18.4 pips over four weeks and 116 pips over six months, which is material at the strategic horizon and immaterial at the tactical one.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months USD liquidity conditions give no directional signal for CAD, and Neutral is a considered conclusion. The structural story is that dollar scarcity is over: the Federal Reserve's balance sheet has stopped shrinking and started growing, up US$127,528m year on year, with the Treasury book expanding US$343,441m — almost entirely in bills, which is reserve-management purchasing rather than stimulus [14]. That removes the mechanism through which quantitative tightening drained global dollar liquidity and pressured non-USD currencies through 2023-2025. Counting against it, reserve balances are down US$300,031m year on year to US$2,924,936m, so the system is converging on the minimum comfortable level of reserves even as the asset side grows — the composition shift toward bills is precisely what a central bank does when it is trying to rebuild reserves without expanding duration. Swap-line usage at US$121m and a SOFR distribution 14 basis points wide on US$2.8tn of volume say the convergence is orderly [14][15]. For CAD specifically the transmission is unusually muted. Canadian banks are deeply integrated with the US financial system, the Bank of Canada holds a standing swap line with the Federal Reserve that has not been needed, and the implied CAD/USD basis residual of approximately -28.8bp is a normal, non-stressed level. The Bank of Canada's own Senior Loan Officer Survey printed -1 against a +1 prior, indicating Canadian lending conditions easing at the margin rather than tightening. Where the dollar goes over six months is a rate-differential and risk-regime question, and both are captured in Factors 1 and 3; loading a directional dollar view into this factor would double-count it. The honest answer is that funding is a non-factor and the stalemate breaks only if reserves fall far enough to force a repo dislocation, which we do not expect inside the horizon.

Norway also runs a +15.59% current account surplus against Canada's -0.87%. The honest caveat is that the trade is late: CAD/NOK at 6.74405 sits at the 7th percentile of its 52-week close range and 3.4% below its 200-day average of 6.97708, with thin two-touch support at 6.68726-6.70879.

cross_horizon_consistency.summary: The tactical stance is Neutral at +0.001 and the strategic stance is mildly Bearish CAD at -0.103 after adversarial verification; the horizons are not aligned and the divergence is mechanistic rather than a modelling artefact.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: Four factors change stance between horizons and every one is driven by the weight schedule interacting with a dated event. Inflation & Growth flips from Bullish at 0.18 weight to Bearish at 0.10 because the tactical window trades the Q2 GDP beat and the 6.4% unemployment rate while the strategic window trades the July 0.0% advance estimate and the Bank's own 0.7% full-year call. Guidance flips from Neutral at 0.07 to Bearish at 0.12 because the tactical window contains only a press conference where tone is unpredictable while the strategic window contains the 2026-10-28 Monetary Policy Report where the Bank must publish numbers that sit behind the market's 2026 hike pricing. Risk Appetite falls from Bullish to Neutral because a VIX at the 2026 low of 14.51 is supportive today and unsustainable as a six-month assumption, and USD Liquidity moves from Bearish to Neutral because the Jackson Hole repricing resolves on 2026-09-16 and then stops being news.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Mid-to-late October 2026, specifically the 2026-10-28 Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report, preceded by the September CPI release around 2026-10-20.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: The arrival of post-tariff Canadian activity data. Section 338 duties took effect 2026-08-22 and Canadian counter-measures on 2026-09-08, but neither appears in the national accounts until the October monthly GDP release covering August and the Q3 national accounts in late November. Until then the data flow still reflects the pre-tariff surge, which is why the tactical horizon remains balanced.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Do not carry a strategic short-CAD position through the tactical window at full size. Hold minimal directional spot exposure into 2026-09-16, use the cheap near-dated volatility surface to own the September event risk, and scale the strategic short-CAD position after the FOMC resolves and into the 2026-10-28 Monetary Policy Report. A CAD rally toward 1.3800 inside the tactical window is a better strategic entry than 1.39045 today.

forward_vs_spot.interpretation: The forward curve implies CAD depreciation of 1.66% annualised, which is simply the carry differential expressed as a price. Our expected path is more bearish CAD than the forwards at every tenor and the gap widens with maturity, from 26 pips at one month to 180 pips at six months; that gap is the quantifiable edge. At three months a correct short-CAD position earns the 138-pip spot edge plus the 57.8 pips already embedded in the forward for a total of 196 pips (1.41% of notional), and 296 pips (2.13%) at six months. Two cautions: the roll premium is observed over a 19.6-to-54.6-day window and extrapolated linearly, so the six-month outright is an approximation rather than a quoted price, and the implied residual of approximately -28.8bp between the -166.3bp roll and the -137.5bp policy differential is attributed to cross-currency basis and term effects as a derived figure.

The tradeable content is entirely in Macklem's press-conference tone: whether he signals that the balance of risks has shifted toward the inflation upside from oil or toward the growth downside from tariffs. The product-level list had not been published as of the valuation date, so the market cannot have priced its composition. Carney called the step reluctant precisely because it raises Canadian costs and reduces choice; with an economy one tenth the size of its counterpart, dollar-for-dollar retaliation is proportionally heavier on Canada.

key_catalysts.event: Statistics Canada Consumer Price Index for August
key_catalysts.rationale: The most important Canadian data point of the tactical window. Headline is at the top of the Bank's 1-3% band entirely because gasoline is up 25.7% year on year; the core measures average exactly 2.0%. If CPI-trim rises toward 2.2%, the oil-broadening risk the Bank said it would respond to becomes live and hike pricing extends. If it slips below 1.9%, the statistical basis for a 2026 hike disappears.

key_catalysts.rationale: The BoJ is at 1.00%, the highest since September 1995, with core inflation at 1.8% and an explicit warning that core will accelerate "clearly above" 2% from the second half of FY2026 on wage pass-through, higher crude and yen depreciation. key_catalysts.rationale: Three decisions on one day, two of which matter for CAD crosses. key_catalysts.rationale: The RBA holds the highest policy rate in the G10 at 4.35%, 210bp above the Bank of Canada, and Australia's REER at 115.92 is up 10.36 points over twelve months — the only currency in the set with positive REER momentum of that scale. key_catalysts.rationale: The first CPI print in which the gasoline base effect turns materially less favourable and the first to capture any tariff-driven price pass-through in both directions — US duties raising Canadian export costs and Canadian counter-duties raising import prices. We expect headline to converge down toward the 2.0% core average as the oil spike anniversaries out, removing the statistical support for the market's ~65% probability of a 2026 hike.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Not priced — the market is extrapolating headline 3.0% rather than modelling the base effect.
key_catalysts.bilateral_relevance: USD/CAD and the Canadian front end.

key_catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report
key_catalysts.rationale: The most important dated event of the strategic horizon and the identified inflection point between our horizons. The Bank must publish a full forecast round incorporating post-tariff activity data, simultaneously marking down 2026 growth for the tariff shock and marking down inflation as gasoline base effects roll off. National Bank and Scotiabank forecast a hike to 2.50% at this meeting; BMO, CIBC, RBC and TD forecast a hold. We expect a hold and a downgraded projection, which is where the ~65% year-end hike pricing comes out of the curve.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Partially — the market prices roughly 65% of a hike by year-end, of which a material share sits at this meeting.
key_catalysts.bilateral_relevance: USD/CAD; all CAD crosses through the carry channel.

If the Bank has not moved by this meeting, the entire 2026 hike premium is removed from the Canadian curve, worth an estimated 15-20bp on the two-year.

A hold with a dovish SEP would begin closing the gap for the first time in a year.

key_catalysts.rationale: A dated, pre-announced escalation that extends the tariff regime from US$20bn and 5.2% of bilateral exports to a materially larger share, striking the auto sector that drove Q2 GDP growth with a 27.0% annualised export surge. Section 338 carries no expiry, so this escalation persists until a presidential proclamation removes it. The Bank of Canada estimates approximately 2 million Canadian jobs depend on goods exports to the United States.

factors_changed.reason: Statistics Canada's July advance GDP estimate printed 0.0% before the Section 338 tariffs took effect, and the Bank's own July MPR carries a 0.7% full-year 2026 growth call that implies materially sub-trend outcomes in the second half.

The 2026-07-29 Summary of Deliberations revealed a Governing Council with an explicit range of views on the sustainability of the rebound and a two-sided commitment to look through oil while refusing to let it become persistent - a posture that produces no tactical signal.

The wedge between market pricing of a ~65% 2026 hike and the Bank's own Q2 Market Participants Survey median of 2.50% in March 2027 was reclassified from a CAD support into the dossier's central identified mispricing. Adversarial verification subsequently corrected the wedge from four quarters to one to two, and the confidence was cut from 58 to 50.

65,515 contracts of combined speculative short covered in the fortnight to 2026-08-25, taking the position from -196,550 to -131,035 while dealers remained net long 124,930, and a record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of Canadian government bonds arrived in Q2.

Record foreign sovereign bond demand, a deficit revised down to C$66.9bn and the lowest net debt-to-GDP in the G7 became a genuine relative-value advantage against deteriorating US and UK fiscal trajectories.

Chair Warsh's 2026-08-28 Jackson Hole address moved September Fed hike odds from 36% to 58%, placing the dollar on the US-exceptionalism side of the smile just as the Bank of Canada is certain to hold.

The Federal Reserve balance sheet expanding US$127.5bn year on year removed the funding tailwind without creating a headwind; residual dollar direction belongs to Factors 1 and 3 rather than being double-counted here.

seasonality.pattern: Two documented patterns fall inside the horizons. First, Canadian Q4 energy hedging: producers routinely hedge forward production through September to November, generating mechanical CAD demand against USD as revenue exposures are converted. Second, the mid-August to mid-October window is historically the weakest stretch of the calendar year for global risk assets, which is CAD-negative through the currency's mild positive risk beta.
seasonality.relevance_window: The energy-hedging flow spans the tactical window and the first half of the strategic window (September to November 2026). The risk-asset seasonal spans the tactical window and expires mid-October 2026. The Canadian federal budget cycle, which the currency brief identifies as CAD-relevant, is a spring event - the Spring Economic Update was tabled 2026-04-28 - and falls outside both horizons.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Not quantifiable from the data available; both patterns are presented as directional biases rather than measured effects. The energy-hedging flow should be larger than a normal September because WTI at US$85.446 and Brent at US$90.135 sit well above the levels at which most 2026 Canadian production was budgeted.
seasonality.current_alignment: The two seasonals offset. Energy hedging is CAD-supportive and unusually strong this year given elevated crude; the risk-asset seasonal is CAD-negative and lands with the VIX at 14.51, its 2026 low, and equities at records - a compressed risk premium entering the historically weakest window. Neither is material relative to the tariff regime, which dominates both.

assumptions: Adversarial verification: this dossier was fact-checked by an independent verification pass before publication. Material corrections applied were the Bank of Canada Q2 2026 Market Participants Survey median (from a first hike in Q3 2027 to a median policy rate of 2.50% in March 2027, narrowing the wedge from four quarters to one to two); the Q1 2026 GDP revision (from '+0.3% annualised from a contraction' to '0.0% to +0.1% quarter on quarter'); the +2.3% investment figure (from aggregate business investment after five declining quarters to engineering structures after two); corporate incomes (+9.7% to +9.6%); the Canadian ten-year (3.746% to 3.74%, with CA-US restated at -102.0bp and 2s10s at +73.0bp); and the speculative short as a share of open interest (63.6% to 39.8% net, 64.9% gross). A BIS citation was added for the real effective exchange rate series. Six factor confidences were lowered, moving the tactical score from +0.007 to +0.001 and the strategic score from -0.114 to -0.103 without changing either stance.

Data hierarchy: where the pipeline data cache holds a precise number it is the source of truth - spot and cross rates, performance, moving averages, realised volatility, ATR, 52-week ranges, support and resistance zones, implied volatility and risk reversals, futures roll premia, all G10 policy rates, the US curve, VIX and credit spreads, commodity levels, the broad dollar index, the point-in-time macro dashboard, CFTC tranches, BIS REER and scheduled central bank decision dates. Web research supplies narrative, guidance, catalysts and citations around those numbers.

Staleness handling: the cached Bank of Canada policy rate of 2.25% as of 2026-08-24 was confirmed against the 2026-07-15 decision, and the 2026-09-02 decision is treated as a catalyst rather than a fact. The cached CFTC tranche of 2026-08-11 was refreshed with the 2026-08-25 reference-date report, with the cached series retained as the trend baseline. Cached sovereign ten-year yields are monthly as of 2026-06-01 and are never quoted as live; live yields for Canada, the US, the UK, Japan, Australia, Germany and Switzerland are sourced to 2026-08-31, while New Zealand, Norwegian and Swedish yields remain on the monthly basis and every spread built from them is labelled mixed-basis.

Valuation methodology: OECD purchasing-power-parity conversion factors are not present in the cache, so the relative-valuation table uses BIS real effective exchange rates as the valuation metric. This is a substitution, not a PPP calculation, and the BIS REER historical percentile of 15 is an estimate against the trailing multi-year range rather than a computed statistic.

Volatility methodology: carry-to-volatility ratios use the policy-rate differential as numerator and the sixty-day realised volatility read directly from the cached derived-pair files as denominator, annualised on 252 weekday observations. Realised volatility is never recomputed and never constructed from two US-dollar legs. The USD/CAD one-year implied-volatility percentile of 22 is an estimate against the pair's typical 4.5-8% band because no quoted implied-vol history was obtained.

Derived figures: the CAD/USD cross-currency basis is derived as the residual between the cache futures-implied roll premium of -166.3bp and the policy differential of -137.5bp, giving approximately -28.8bp. Forward outrights at one, three and six months are extrapolated linearly from a roll premium observed over a 19.6-to-54.6-day window, so the six-month outright is an approximation rather than a quoted price. Cross-pair futures roll premia use contract-dependent sign conventions and are not relied upon for directional inference; only the USD/CAD figure is used.

Documented data gaps: quoted three-month EUR/USD, JPY/USD and GBP/USD cross-currency basis; quoted OIS-implied Bank of Canada rate levels (only probability commentary available); a live WCS-WTI spot differential (only Alberta Energy Regulator and CAPP forecast vintages, labelled best available at approximately US$12/bbl for 2026); a Canadian sovereign CDS spread; a Citi Economic Surprise Index for Canada (the cached calendar surprise ledger is used instead); implied volatility for CAD/NOK, CAD/SEK and CAD/SGD; and the Bank of Canada CERI effective index.

Macro comparison table caveats: core CPI is not carried in the cache for USD, EUR, GBP, CHF, AUD, NZD or SEK, so the headline vintage is repeated in the core field and flagged in the measure name. Cached euro-area, Swiss, Swedish and Norwegian CPI vintages are 2025-Q4 and are labelled stale; live Norwegian figures (3.0% headline, 2.7% CPI-ATE for July 2026) are substituted and cited. SGD has no cached vintages because Singapore is not an OECD member; the GDP, unemployment and current account fields carry zero as a placeholder, which is a documented gap and not a measurement.

Source conflicts: two Japanese July 2026 CPI figures were encountered, 1.9% headline from Trading Economics and 3.1% from a secondary headline. The Trading Economics series is used, the conflict is disclosed, and confidence on the Japanese comparison is reduced accordingly.
Quote convention: USD/CAD is quoted as Canadian dollars per US dollar. A rising USD/CAD is a weaker CAD. Bullish CAD means USD/CAD falling; Bearish CAD means USD/CAD rising.

Figures the verification pass could not confirm are labelled best available and flagged in the text: the entire cache-sourced volatility surface, realised-vol series, moving averages, 52-week range and touch-counted structural zones; forward points and outrights; the WCS-WTI differential; the Ivey and manufacturing PMI levels; the August calendar surprise ledger; the participation rate and average weekly earnings; and the 76% (2024) and 72% (2025) US export-share comparators. Citation 27 (Market Participants Survey, field dates mid-June) and citation 28 (Financial Stability Report, published 2026-05-28) sit outside the 60-day strategic freshness window and are disclosed as such; citations 11, 12, 32, 34 and 37 are rolling pages whose quoted values will not reproduce on re-check.
